title: One Server to Rule Them All
summary: Everything runs through one app server. It handles today's load, but when it dies, so does the product.
scenario: A small SaaS app serves 900 requests per second through a single app server. Capacity looks fine: utilization is about 60%.
Last week that server was rebooted for a kernel patch and the whole product went down for 4 minutes. Customers noticed.
Make the system survive the loss of any one component, without blowing the budget. The NoSQL database is already replicated.
hints: Run the simulation and look at Single points of failure. The simulator fails each component in turn and measures how much traffic loses its path.
Redundancy means more than one of something, plus a way to route around the broken one. Raise the app server's replicas, or add a second app server.
If you put a Load Balancer in front, it becomes the new single point of failure, so give it 2 replicas too. Two of everything still fits under $800.
explanation: A single point of failure (SPOF) is any component whose loss takes down a meaningful share of traffic. Spare capacity doesn't help if there is only one instance.
The fix is N+1 redundancy: at least two instances behind something that health-checks them and stops sending traffic to a dead one. That is the load balancer's real job, beyond spreading load.
Watch for the SPOF you just added. A single load balancer is itself a SPOF, which is why production setups run LBs in pairs or use a managed, multi-zone LB.
Redundancy costs money, so size the survivors to carry the full load alone. Here one app server can handle 900 rps, so two give you N+1 at about double the compute cost.
